rows: Rear vent back wall (3112 B / 3142 B)

steps: Codes & site check
Install to CAN/CSA-B365 and local codes; check with building officials first. Not in any fireplace, and never connected to an air distribution duct or system.

The installation must conform to CAN/CSA-B365, Installation Code for Solid-Fuel-Burning Appliances and Equipment. Local building officials have final authority to approve the installation; discuss it with them before you begin.

  • Do not install in any fireplace.
  • Do not connect to any air distribution duct or system.
  • Confirm the stove and connector meet all clearances to combustibles, and that floor protection is adequate.

The data plate on the back of the stove gives the safety testing information, the certified testing laboratory and the installation requirements.
Unpack, check, fit legs
Check the center grate and fire bricks haven't shifted and the air control works freely. Two-person lift. 3112 B: bolt the legs on; 3142 B: lift into position.

After unpacking, check that the center grate and the fire bricks are firmly in position and the air control works freely. The stove is heavy: lift it with two people.

3112 B: fit the legs

  1. Flatten the outer packaging on the floor next to the stove as a protective work surface.
  2. Take the legs and bolts out of the stove.
  3. Lay the stove gently on its back and unscrew it from the wooden pallet.
  4. Bolt the legs to the underside of the base with the bolts supplied.
  5. Lift the stove upright, avoiding excess load on the back legs.

3142 B

After removing the outer packaging, lift the stove into position.
Baffles & accessories
Seat the upper baffle plate on the rear (fixed) baffle against the 2 cast lugs. The access baffle must always be fitted. Poker, flue gasket and riddling tool are in the ashpan or firebox.

The upper baffle plate sits on top of the rear (fixed) baffle section, secured against the 2 upstanding cast lugs.

The access baffle must always be fitted when the stove is in use: it assists combustion and protects the top plate.

Standard accessories (poker, ceramic flue connection gasket, riddling tool) are usually in the ashpan or firebox area.
Chimney
Residential masonry or listed type HT chimney (UL-103-1985 / ULC S-629), one flue per appliance, not less than 6" internal. Support it independently of the stove.

Use a residential type masonry or listed type HT factory-built chimney: UL-103-1985 (2100º F.) in the USA, ULC S-629 (650ºC) in Canada.

  • Chimney and connector not less than 6 inches diameter (or equivalent cross section), and not significantly larger: too large a section lets flue gases cool and makes the stove sluggish or unpredictable.
  • Do not connect to a flue serving any other appliance; one flueway per appliance.
  • The flue system must be independently secured and must not rely on the stove for support. Do not install the chimney directly at the appliance outlet.
  • Seal all connections so the system is airtight from the heater to the chimney outlet.

Chimney height: Morsø recommends (but does not require) a chimney system at least 16 feet above the stove in normal domestic situations, measured from the flue collar to the top of the chimney (p. 5). The minimum height for a good draft is 12 ft above the stove, clear of the spine of the roof (p. 16).
Top or rear flue exit

Ships with the flue collar on the top plate and a blanking plate on the rear exit. For a rear exit, knock out the rear convection panel plate, move the blanking plate to the top and bolt the collar to the rear outlet.

1. Knock out the top steel plate in the rear heat convection panel with gentle hammer taps on the small "bridges" in the circular cut-outs.
  2. Unbolt the cast iron blanking plate and install it into the top of the stove.
  3. Bolt the flue collar over the rear flue outlet using the bolts and clamps provided.

The blanking plate also works as an extra clean-out access during the annual cleaning. Wear gloves and protective eyewear when drilling, cutting or joining connector sections.
Chimney connector
6" (150mm) connector: 24 MSG black or blue single-wall or listed double-wall, never galvanized. Min. three screws per joint; horizontal runs rise 1/4" per ft.

• The connector must be 6 inches (150mm) in diameter.
  • Single-wall: 24 MSG black or blue, 24 gauge or heavier steel. Double-wall: tested and listed for solid fuel. No galvanized connector.
  • Secure with a minimum of three screws to the stove and to each adjoining section.
  • Horizontal runs: 18 inches from the ceiling, no more than two 90 degree turns, sloping upward 1/4 inch per foot (20 mm per metre) toward the chimney. Recommended maximum horizontal run 3 feet (1 metre); total length no longer than 8 feet (2.5 metres).
  • Use mild bends (45º rather than 90º). Keep all parts of the venting accessible for cleaning.
  • Not through an attic, closet or similar concealed space; avoid combustible walls and ceilings where possible.
Clearances
Set unit and connector distances from the per-model tables: single-wall, double-wall, rear vent and alcove. 4" or more to non-combustibles is recommended.
Floor protection
Non-combustible ember pad beneath the stove: US 16" to the front and 6" to the sides of the loading door and ash openings; Canada 450 mm on door sides, 200 mm elsewhere.
Combustion air & mobile homes
Fresh-air inlet of 2 square inches (1250 square mm) if the room is tight. US mobile homes: outside air kit, HT connector and chimney, spark-arrestor cap, stove bolted down.
First fire
Keep the initial fire small so the paint cures and the plates settle; ventilate the paint fumes. Never alter the factory-set minimum low burn rate.

panels.title: Smoke spills or fire won't respond
items: Poor draft is almost certainly to blame; rarely, too little fresh air reaching the room
Chimney cold or poorly insulated, warm weather, or no wind (cold chimney: burning a rolled-up newspaper in the cleaning door may help)
Chimney too short, sitting in the lee of the roof or tall trees
Air leaking in at cracked joints, the cleaning door or flue pipe; unsealed unused fireplaces on the chimney
Flue pipe or chimney clogged with soot; house sealed too tightly

panels.title: Over-firing
items: Flue temperature over 450° C (750°F) in the stove pipe
Overly strong draft → excessive temperatures, short burn times
Baffle distorted by an over-fire → efficiency compromised; replace

panels.title: Sooty or misting glass
items: Fuel too wet (wood spits or sizzles, glass persistently mists up)
Logs too large or not split
Combustion temperatures too low, or stove run too slowly

panels.title: Sluggish fire or fast wear
items: Overly dry, gray wood → back-puffing and sluggishness
Sudden sluggishness → soot fall around the flue collar or in the flue
Hardened door gasket → air leaks, fire less controllable
Persistent heavy firing, or soot and ash left to accumulate → fast internal wear

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Morsø recommends the "top-down" method. It's the most environmentally friendly way to light, and it minimizes soot on the glass.

  1. Lay about 2-4 lbs of dry kindling sticks. Put two firelighters directly under the top layer of kindling.
  2. Open the air fully: move the air control handle all the way down. Light the fire.
  3. Close the door most of the way, leaving it open an inch or two so the fire gets plenty of air.
  4. After 5-10 minutes, when the chimney has warmed through, close the door. A good bed of embers forms in another 15-20 minutes.
Stay close while it lights. Never leave the stove unattended with the door open. Once it's going, run it with the door fully closed.

The very first fire

Keep it small so the paint can cure and the main plates can settle into position. The paint gives off some fumes, so ventilate the room. For that first lighting, a 5-6 inch layer (2-4 pound) of dry kindling builds a bed of ash.

Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
You control the fire with one lever: the primary air control, under the ash lip of the stove.

Handle all the way downFully open: lighting, and right after reloading
Handle midwayMedium burn
Handle horizontalClosed

Opening it lets preheated air into the firebox through the "airwash" above the glass. Secondary air comes in through the baffle at the back of the firebox. It's fixed open and can't be adjusted. The air control on the door is fixed too; it's only decoration.

Rules of thumb

  • Less heat: less wood, less air. More heat: more wood, more air. Keep a good layer of embers either way.
  • Most modern wood stoves run best and most efficiently at medium to medium-low burn rates.
  • The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory. Altering it is against federal regulations.
  • Never try to get a bigger fire by altering the air control's adjustment range.

The stove has a removable handle for extra safety. When you're not using it, store it on the lug behind the right leg of the stove.

reload.title: Reloading the stove
reload.html:
Reload while there are still plenty of live embers, adding a modest layer of wood each time.

  1. Use the poker to spread the embers across the firebox floor, with plenty toward the front.
  2. Lay three pieces of wood on the embers, half an inch (1 cm) or more apart. Point the log ends toward the opening, but not too close to the front. Each log should be about 10-12" long and weigh about 2 lb.
  3. Close the door. Leave the air fully open.
  4. After a few minutes, set the air for the heat you want. For a medium burn, put the handle midway between closed and fully open.

Make sure there's a good layer of embers before you add wood. The new wood should catch within 2 minutes. Logs that don't ignite can, in an extreme case, make the flue gases ignite, which risks damage or injury.

Most wood per load2.5 kg/h / 5.5 lbs (approx. 3 split logs)
Quick guide (back page)2 - 3 pieces, no more than 2 - 2.5 kg
Enough air shows as clear, yellow flames. Morsø's safe-heating page also says: never burn overnight.

wood.title: Choosing your wood
wood.html:
Burn only natural, untreated wood that is well seasoned and dry. The stove is listed for wood only.

Length12 inches (30 cm) max
Thicknessapprox. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm)
Weight per piecearound 2 lbs
Moistureno more than 20%
Note: p. 11 gives the split size as approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm) in section; p. 28 says the fuel must be split and 8 - 12 cm thick.

Split logs down the middle so moisture can escape. Stack them under cover where air moves through. Soft woods may season in one good summer; oak, maple and elm can take up to 18 months. The Morsø Moisture Meter (part # 62929900) checks moisture.

Seasoned wood feels light and cracks from the center out at the ends. If it spits or sizzles and the glass keeps misting up, it's too wet. Very dry, gray wood can cause back-puffing and a sluggish fire.

Never burn

Garbage; lawn clippings or yard waste; materials containing rubber, including tires; materials containing plastic; waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, or asphalt products; materials containing asbestos; construction or demolition debris; railroad ties or pressure-treated wood; manure or animal remains; salt-water driftwood or other previously salt-water saturated materials; unseasoned wood; paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the heater ineffective and cause smoke. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust, wax or similar substances are still fine for starting a fire.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
If you run the stove at the right temperatures, the glass stays mostly clean. Dirt that settles while lighting usually burns off as the stove heats up.

For heavier deposits

  • Wait until the glass is cold. Never clean it while hot.
  • Use Morsø glass cleaner, following its instructions.
  • Never use abrasive cleaners on the glass.

Why it got dirty

Wood that's too wet, logs too large or not split, or a fire burning too cool. Running the stove too slowly also leaves soot.

Cracked or broken glass? Don't use the stove. Replace it right away with Morsø high-temperature ceramic glass from your dealer. To avoid breaks, don't strike the glass or slam the door.

Old ceramic glass can't go in ordinary glass recycling. Hand it in at a recycling station as ceramic glass.

The painted body

Vacuum it with a soft brush attachment or wipe it with a lint-free cloth. If the paint turns slightly gray over time, Morsø touch-up spray paint renews it. Expect a slight smell the first time you fire it after touching up, so ventilate the room.

ash.title: Emptying the ash
ash.html:
Empty the ash pan daily, or as needed. Ash piled up to the underside of the grate traps heat and can make the grate fail early. Do keep a 1-1.5 inch (2-3 cm) layer of ash on the firebox floor.

  1. With the door closed, work the grate with the riddling bar.
  2. Open the door and stir excess ash through the grate slots into the pan with a shovel or the poker.
  3. Lift the pan out, keeping it level.
  4. Empty it into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set that on a noncombustible floor or the ground, well away from anything that burns, and keep it closed until the cinders are cold.
  5. Put the pan back and close the door.
Never empty the stove while it's in operation, and never use a household or shop vacuum on the ash.

End of the season

Clean the stove out thoroughly: leftover ash soaks up moisture, and that causes rust. A moisture absorber such as kitty litter in the ash pan helps over summer; remove it before the heating season. Fit a chimney cap against rain, but don't block the flue completely.

Note: p. 20 says to leave "the spinner" slightly open to allow airflow when the stove is left unused; p. 13 says the air control on the door is fixed and only decorative.

chimney.title: Chimney care & the yearly check
chimney.html:
Burning wood slowly makes tar and vapors that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire.

How often

  • Check for soot above the baffle plate and around the flue outlet about once a month at first.
  • Inspect the stove pipe and chimney regularly during the heating season for creosote buildup.
  • If the fire suddenly turns sluggish, check for fallen soot around the flue collar or in the chimney.
  • Clean the chimney after each heating season, and inspect it before the next for bird's nests or blockages.

Sweeping

Let the stove cool completely, then look up through the flue collar with a mirror. Use a brush the same size and shape as the flue liner; deposits fall to the clean-out door. Clean pipe sections outside with a stiff wire brush and refit them with sheet metal screws. Or call your Morsø dealer or a chimney sweep.

Before each season

Also check the chimney and pipe for damage, the gaskets for wear, the glass for cracks, and the door and handles for tightness. Replace the door gasket if the door gets hard to close or air leaks in. Grease the hinges and closing parts once a year with copper grease or another heat-resistant grease.

Chimney fire? Close the air control. Get everyone out of the house. Call the fire department.

overfire.title: Over-firing: how hot is too hot
overfire.html:
Do not over-fire the stove. Over-firing means burning the stove too hot. It can cause a house fire or permanently damage the stove.

If any part of the stove or the stove pipe glows, you are over-firing.

Watch the flue temperature

Normal averageapprox. 300° C (550°F)
Must not exceed450° C (750°F)

These are flue temperatures in the stove pipe; the normal average is measured 20 cm above the stove. Going over the limit counts as over-firing and may wear the stove out early. The Morsø Flue Gas Thermometer (part # 62901200) attaches magnetically to the pipe about 20 cm (8") above the top plate and reads its surface temperature.

Note: p. 15 gives the normal average flue temperature as approx. 300° C (550°F) and the limit as 450° C (750°F); the Celsius and Fahrenheit figures in each pair aren't equivalent.

Avoid it

  • Load no more than 2.5 kg/h / 5.5 lbs of wood, approx. 3 split logs.
  • Never try to boost the fire by altering the air control's range.
  • A very strong chimney draft can also cause excessive temperatures and short burn times.

Persistent heavy firing wears the inside out fast. A baffle bent by over-firing still works, but less efficiently; replace it as soon as possible.

safety.title: Safety around the stove
safety.html:
• The stove is hot while in operation. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; touching it can burn skin.
  • Run it with the door fully closed. Never leave it unattended with the door open: gas and flame can be drawn out of the opening.
  • Keep furniture at least 30 inches away. Keep drying clothes, newspapers, firewood and other movable things that burn 30 inches away too.
  • Keep gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid and similar liquids away from the stove while it's in use.
  • Wear safety goggles and gloves when you do maintenance.

Carbon monoxide

Almost all fires make some carbon monoxide (CO), a toxic gas. The tested CO emission rate for the 3100 B series is 0.93 g/min. You greatly reduce CO by keeping a well-established fire and avoiding a smouldering, smoky one. Morsø highly recommends a CO detector in the same room as the stove.

Smoke detectors

Some areas require smoke and CO detectors. Put at least one smoke detector on each floor, away from the stove and close to sleeping areas; one too close can go off when you reload. Morsø also recommends a smoke detector in the room where the stove is installed.

warranty.title: The Morsø guarantee
warranty.html:
Morsø offers a 10-Year Manufacturers Guarantee against manufacturing defects in any of the main exterior body parts of the stove. It applies when the stove was supplied by an authorised Morsø dealer.

Not covered

  • The flame-path parts that take the fire's heat: ashpan, grate, firebricks, glass, baffle and flue collar. These may need replacing from time to time as routine maintenance.
  • The ceramic rope (gasket).
  • The paint finish.

Register your new stove online; the guarantee page of the manual gives the web address and explains the guarantee and product registration card.

Always use original Morsø spare parts. Your Morsø dealer sells the service parts, and Morsø recommends replacing damaged ones as soon as possible to avoid collateral damage.

specOutput.html:
Heat output (test range)9,199 to 28,000 Btu's

One rating covers both models; the manual gives no separate output or efficiency figures for the 3112 B and 3142 B. Listed for burning wood only. The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered (federal regulation).

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
Meets CAN/ULC-S627 for installation on a combustible floor; no radiant floor protection is required. A non-combustible pad for falling embers is.

US · front16"
US · right / left side6"
US · backnone listed
Canada · front450 mm
Canada · back / sides200 mm

US: non-combustible material beneath the heater, extending 16" to the front and 6" to the sides of the fuel loading door and ash removal openings.

Canada (CSA B365): continuous, durable, non-combustible pad beneath the appliance, at least 450 mm (18 in) beyond any side with a door, for the full width plus 200 mm (8 in) each side, and 200 mm (8 in) beyond other sides. Installed less than 200 mm (8 in) from a wall, the pad need only reach the base of the wall. Not on carpet unless structurally supported against displacement and distortion.

specAir.title: Combustion air & mobile homes
specAir.html:
Fresh-air inlet

Needed unless enough air leaks into the room through doorways, windows and the like; most important in a well-sealed room or where an extractor hood or ventilation system disturbs the air pressure.

Free air space2 square inches (1250 square mm)

Not on a wall usually under negative pressure from normal wind patterns, and not directly across the room from the stove (cold draft).

Mobile home (USA only)

  • Outside combustion air kit (install per the kit's guide) and terminal cap with spark arrestor.
  • Listed Type HT chimney connector and HT chimney; never a single-wall connector (stovepipe).
  • Bolt the stove through the hearth pad into the flooring; follow the floor protection requirements precisely.
  • Intake air through the floor into a vented crawl space, or through the wall.
  • Install per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD). Top chimney sections must be removable for a maximum clearance of 13.5' from ground level for transport.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of floor, walls and ceiling/roof: don't cut joists, studs or trusses.
Never draw combustion air from a wall, floor or ceiling cavity or an enclosed space such as an attic or garage. Do not install in a sleeping room. Canada: do not install in a transportable building or mobile home.

conflicts.issue: Chimney height: p. 5 recommends at least 16 feet above the stove (flue collar to chimney top, 'not required'); p. 16 gives proper height as 'Minimum 12 ft. above the stove'. Also shown in step3.
conflicts.reason: p. 5's 16 feet is a recommendation the manual marks 'not required'; p. 16's 12 ft is the minimum height for a good draft. A recommended height and a minimum fit together; both are now stated plainly in specFlue and step3.

conflicts.issue: Split size: p. 11 says approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm) in section; p. 28 says split and 8 - 12 cm thick. Also shown in specFuel.
Flue temperatures on p. 15 pair 300° C with 550°F and 450° C with 750°F; the Celsius and Fahrenheit figures are not equivalent, so the limit to read on a thermometer is unclear.
Idle-period care says to leave 'the spinner' slightly open (p. 20); no spinner is described anywhere else, and p. 13 says the lower air control on the door is fixed and decorative.

review.notes: Physical pages match the printed page numbers. How the manual distinguishes the models: clearance tables (pp. 8-9, 3142 B consistently smaller), leg fitting (3112 B legs bolted on, 3142 B lifted into position, p. 4), parts list (different base plate and side plate; side plate convection, washer, pinol screw and distance tube pos. 83-86 only on the 3142 B, pp. 23-24) and separate parts diagrams (pp. 21-22; the p. 22 title block reads 'Morsø 3412 B US-CAN'). Output, efficiency, CO rate, fuel, flue and floor-protection figures are given once for both models. Pages 7, 25 and 26 have no extractable text (probably figures); p. 6 refers to 'Wall Pass-Throughs' sections that are not in the text. Clearance letters A-H are transcribed from the tables' own text labels; the diagrams were not reconstructed. The 3142 B single-wall back clearance prints 9" as 228 mm; elsewhere 9" is 229 mm (shown as printed). The manual gives no heating area, firebox volume, dimensions or weight, so those catalog specs could not be checked; catalog features mention tertiary air, but the manual describes only primary (airwash) and fixed secondary air. Left out of the guide: p. 5 says 'A chimney connector is included with the heater' although the standard accessories listed are poker, ceramic flue connection gasket and riddling tool; the p. 10 mobile-home caution not to use a grate to elevate the fire (the stove has a riddling grate); and the unclear p. 18 sentence about scraping out the 'old fire furnace' before refitting the baffle.
